# The Moonshot {#sec-moonshot}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"The purpose of computing is insight, not numbers."*
>
> –  Richard Hamming, *Numerical Methods for Scientists and Engineers* (1962) [@Hamming1962NumericalMethods]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** Richard Hamming, a pioneer in computer science, argued that
computing should yield insight rather than raw data. The distinction matters
here. AI-assisted architecture should help architects ask better questions,
test alternatives, explain mechanisms, and defend decisions. Producing more
candidates is useful only when it improves that work.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
What would it take to build an AI-assisted capability that carries compact
system intent through real system-and-chip design to a supported architecture
result, rather than merely generating artifacts faster?
:::

Computer architecture has repeatedly expanded what we can design by advancing our methods alongside our devices. Lasting advances do more than automate a local step; they give us better abstractions, repeatable paths to design artifacts, and checks that expose bad results. That history sets the standard for judging AI-assisted design.

AI is a possibility, not a guarantee of better architecture. While learned methods can process unstructured information, propose and screen alternatives, and coordinate actions across tools, these abilities alone do not make the resulting artifacts correct, physically realizable, or architecturally useful.

This standard defines an ambitious, testable moonshot. It asks whether a complete design system carry compact system intent through alternatives, tools, measurements, and checks until it supports a verifiable hardware-and-software architecture result? The target is not autonomous prompt-to-chip generation. The added complexity and cost of AI are justified only if the complete approach genuinely improves our architecture work.

The Lighthouse request grounds this moonshot in a low-power mobile XR subsystem. Its short statement hides a full-stack architecture study across workloads, software, hardware, and physical implementation. It forces us to ask whether AI changes architecture practice or merely accelerates a local task.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, we can:

- Define the Architecture 2.0 moonshot and AI-assisted design capabilities.
- Translate compact system intent into explicit cross-stack architecture specifications.
- Distinguish generated artifacts from verifiable architecture results.
- Evaluate architecture quality and design efficacy as independent tests.
:::

## Historical Context and Paradigm Shifts

### Historical Design Method Progressions

Looking back at familiar transitions, we can see how new methods have historically expanded what we can design as computer architects. The Mead–Conway VLSI methodology[^fn-vlsi-complexity-c01] gave us a way to connect abstractions and design rules with automated tools, fabrication access, and teaching [@MeadConway1980VLSI]. When reduced-instruction-set computing arrived, it fundamentally reshaped our hardware–software contract around a tight set of principles we could test quantitatively, establishing a foundation that today enables 64-bit RISC-V application processors to be evaluated on canonical instruction set simulators like Spike [@PattersonDitzel1980RISC]. Later, logic synthesis allowed us to practically transform register-transfer-level descriptions directly into gate-level implementations, while fast open-source C++ cycle-accurate HDL simulators like Verilator, along with formal timing analysis and equivalence checking tools like Synopsys Formality, caught our mistakes and exposed bad outputs [@DeMicheli1994SynthesisOptimization; @Formality]. In each of these eras, an idea became truly consequential because we could systematically apply, inspect, and improve the methodology built around it.

[^fn-vlsi-complexity-c01]: **VLSI complexity (origin)**: Early-1980s frontier microprocessors held about $10^4$ to $10^5$ transistors, and by 2021 frontier chips held tens of billions [@Rupp2022MicroprocessorTrendData]. Mead and Conway answered that outgrowth of transistor-level practice with higher-level abstractions, design rules, and fabrication access that a course could teach and a community could share.

While we relied on different technical mechanisms for each of these transformations, they all expanded the fundamental unit of design we could express. Just as importantly, they made the resulting objects checkable against shared rules, tools, or measurements (@fig-design-method-progression).

![**New design methods expand what we can express and check.** Established advances connect an input abstraction to a larger design object and to the checks or infrastructure that make the transformation dependable. We show AI-assisted architecture separately as a prospective system for carrying our system intent and current project state to a supported architecture result through existing tools and checks.](images/F1d-design-method-progression){#fig-design-method-progression width="100%" fig-alt="Historical progression through Mead-Conway design rules and abstractions, the RISC hardware-software contract, RTL logic synthesis, and reusable hardware generators. Each established method connects an input abstraction to a design object and a dependable check or infrastructure. A separate prospective case shows an AI-assisted design system connecting system intent and current project state through existing tools and checks to a supported comparison or finding with stated alternatives and limits; the result may reject a candidate or retain the reference design."}

In our diagram, the established rows trace our progress from shared design rules up to parameterized hardware generators [@Izraelevitz2017Chisel], with every stage pairing a broader design object with external checks. The prospective row stands apart because we have yet to prove its much stronger claim. It asks whether we can build a design system that reliably connects our high-level intent and current project state to a supported architecture result, all without weakening the rigorous tools and checks we depend on. We should view this not as an inevitable next step, nor as a magical prompt-to-chip pipeline, but as an open challenge.

When we measure our current AI capabilities against those historical transitions, we find that merely generating more code, RTL, or design proposals might be useful, but it does not by itself give us a new design method. Our real challenge is figuring out how to carry our intent seamlessly across workloads, software, hardware, and physical implementations, all while radically reducing the human effort we spend exploring and checking alternatives. We refer to this long-range ambition as an *architecture moonshot*.

> **Architecture moonshot.** An architecture moonshot is a difficult,
> long-term target that existing tools and design practice cannot yet address
> end to end. It seeks a major improvement in how architects turn system and
> chip design questions into supported results and decisions. Advances in AI,
> data, or tools must make at least part of the target practical to investigate
> without implying that the whole problem has been solved.

For us to treat an architecture moonshot credibly, three things must align. These comprise an important architecture problem, a substantial shift in our design practice, and a demonstrated advance that actually makes meaningful progress possible (@fig-moonshot-venn).

![**A moonshot becomes testable only when all three conditions hold.** A major architecture challenge and a proposed change in our design practice require a demonstrated advance in AI, data, or tools that makes meaningful progress practical.](images/F1c-moonshot-venn){#fig-moonshot-venn width="85%" fig-alt="Three-circle Venn diagram showing an architecture moonshot at the intersection of a grand architecture challenge, a substantial change in design practice, and an enabling advance in AI, data, or tools."}

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

Each of these conditions protects us against a specific mode of failure. When we tackle a difficult problem without a new method, we just end up with an unsolved problem. If we propose a new method without demonstrating an enabling capability, we are merely sharing an aspiration. And when we showcase an enabling advance with no real architecture problem behind it, we are left with nothing more than a capability demonstration. Our research must prove that advances in AI, data, or tools make a meaningful part of the target practical, rather than simply inferring that capability from our ambitions alone.

We can look to Explicitly Parallel Instruction Computing (EPIC), the basis of the Itanium processor, as a concrete example of the risks tied to unproven moonshot dependencies. With EPIC, we shifted much of our scheduling responsibility onto the compiler, making compiler-exposed parallelism the central pillar of the architecture [@SchlanskerRau2000EPIC].

::: {.callout-war-story title="EPIC shows why a moonshot must name its dependency"}
**The claim.** EPIC exposed instruction-level parallelism in the ISA so
the compiler could schedule operations explicitly.

**The gap.** The expected benefit depended on the compiler finding and
scheduling enough useful parallelism despite control flow, aliasing, memory
behavior, and the available software path.

**The lesson.** A moonshot can fail when it depends on a capability whose
limits become clear only after large commitments. AI-assisted architecture
faces the same risk if it assumes that plausible generation will become
physically valid system design without demonstrating the required knowledge,
tool use, and checks.
:::

The takeaway for us is not that we should avoid ambitious targets. Instead, we must clearly state what capability our target depends on and identify exactly what results would challenge our assumptions. To rigorously test those dependencies in our own work with the Lighthouse, we first need to place AI squarely within established design automation and clearly name the components we expect to perform the heavy lifting.
### AI as Design Automation

When we turn design intent into actual artifacts and results under tight
constraints, we rely on design automation, incorporating the models, algorithms, and tools
that make our ideas real. We already automate substantial parts of our
architecture work through logic synthesis, parameterized generators,
design-space search, and rigorous verification. Today, researchers and engineers
are weaving learned methods into that established practice, taking on everything
from exploring the design space to optimizing physical placement
[@WangEtAl2026AgentDSE; @MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. Crucially, these new
methods extend our existing automation rather than replacing the trusted tools
that make our designs executable and checkable.

In this book, we use the term *AI* to name a broad discipline and a set of
learned techniques, rather than a single component. These techniques offer us
prediction, generation, optimization, and other specialized capabilities. When
we build an AI-assisted system, we integrate these learned methods directly with
our conventional analysis and design tools.

The inputs, outputs, and applications of a model ultimately dictate the work it
can do for us. For instance, a *learned model* derives its behavior from
examples, saving us from writing every rule explicitly. We use a *predictor* to
estimate properties that are too expensive or difficult to measure directly – such as using McPAT, an integrated framework for power, area, and timing estimation, to model physical microarchitectural footprints – while a *generator* proposes new artifacts or design candidates. When we need to
improve a specific objective by choosing among alternatives, we turn to an
*optimizer*. *Retrieval* helps us find relevant information within a large body
of material. While classical definitions often describe an *agent* simply as an
entity perceiving and acting within an environment [@RussellNorvig2020AIMA], we
set a stricter operational bar for architecture assistance. For us, an agent
must take actions, observe the environment's response, and adapt its next move
based on that feedback. Simply answering a prompt doesn't make a model an agent,
just as calling several tools doesn't make a fixed script one.

We make these distinctions to clarify capabilities, not to assign authority.
While generation, prediction, and optimization represent broad families of
methods, our daily work involves specific roles, including proposing candidates,
estimating consequences, selecting experiments, repairing artifacts, and
checking properties. A single method might juggle several of these roles, just
as a given role might be handled by a learned model, a conventional algorithm, a
trusty design tool, or an architect like you. Ultimately, the assigned role, not
the "AI" label, dictates exactly what a component must produce and how rigorously
we must check its output.

Our history with AI in architecture reaches back much further than today's
generative systems. We have long relied on learned predictors, surrogate models,
reinforcement learning, and autotuning for tasks like branch prediction,
prefetching, system control, and design-space exploration
[@ChenPenneyJimenez2020AIArchitecture; @JimenezLin2001Perceptron;
@IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE; @LeeBrooks2006RegressionModeling;
@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM; @AnselEtAl2014OpenTuner]. While recent language and
generative models undeniably expand the types of artifacts and information we
can manipulate [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo; @HeEtAl2024ChatEDA], this historical
continuity matters. We can embed learned mechanisms like branch predictors
directly into the systems we design, or we can use surrogate models and
autotuners to help us actually conduct our design work. Here, our focus remains
firmly on that second application. Because architecture already blends our human
judgment with an arsenal of simulators, compilers, scripts, and verification
tools, the real question we face today is where learned methods can meaningfully
elevate that complete practice.

Bringing these methods into architecture brings us face-to-face with immediate
practical limits. Often, our project-specific specifications, implementation
data, and internal tool results simply do not exist in public training corpora;
ChipNeMo, for example, leans heavily on proprietary chip-design data and
internal evaluations [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo]. Furthermore, the computational
feedback required to reject a bad candidate can be prohibitively expensive.
BOOM-Explorer takes hours just to evaluate one sample in its implementation flow
[@BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer], much like cycle-accurate microarchitectural simulations in gem5 require significant runtime per candidate [@BinkertEtAl2011Gem5], and industry surveys constantly remind us that
verification consumes a massive share of our engineering effort
[@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. Even the model inference itself burns
compute and injects its own latency, which is exactly why inference benchmarks
rigorously measure latency and throughput [@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf]. When we
embark on an AI-assisted study, the total effort encompasses data preparation,
tool feedback, rigorous verification, and model inference. Merely generating or
ranking a candidate is only a fraction of our overall work.
## The Architecture Moonshot Brief

### The Mobile XR Subsystem Case Study

We kick off the Lighthouse with a straightforward product request. When we unpack this brief prompt, we uncover work spanning the entire design stack, making the true difficulty of AI-assisted architecture crystal clear. While data and evaluation costs are important parts of our study, as architects, our first job is figuring out what this request actually demands. We will use this same core request as a running example throughout the book.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The Lighthouse request"}
Design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for an XRBench-class
real-time mobile XR workload. Realize it as a vector-capable CPU, accelerator,
or SoC block under a 3\ W TDP target in a 3\ nm-class LP mobile process, and
return a design-space report with evidence and rejected alternatives.
:::

We call this our *Lighthouse prompt*. For context, XR stands for extended reality, TDP is thermal design power, and LP simply means a low-power process. We've chosen XRBench because it offers a well-known public suite of mobile XR workloads, rather than a rigid, locked-down product specification [@KwonEtAl2023XRBench]. When we operate at this scale, our prompt deliberately flushes out the deep architectural work that a smaller, simpler generation task would obscure. It gives us a solid, long-term target for measuring our progress against the full design challenge.

Underneath this brief prompt lies a complete hardware-and-software SoC architecture. Physically, the subsystem must fit within a tight 3\ W sustained Thermal Design Power (TDP) envelope in a passive optical frame HMD form factor, operating under strict skin-temperature ceilings (< 41\ °C) in a 3\ nm-class low-power (LP) process node. Architecturally, the compute substrate requires a 64-bit RISC-V application processor core (RV64GCV) equipped with a 128-bit RVV 1.0 vector execution pipeline for data-parallel math, alongside a dedicated NPU matrix engine (a systolic tensor array) optimized for spatial perception (visual-inertial odometry, depth mapping, gaze tracking) and neural rendering re-projection (NeRF/Gaussian Splatting). Memory traffic must be carefully managed across a multi-level hierarchy – 32\ KB L1 caches, a 512\ KB private L2 cache, a 4\ MB shared system-level L3 cache, and tightly coupled TCM scratchpads – linked over an AMBA AXI5 on-chip interconnect and UCIe (Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express) die-to-die interfaces to high-bandwidth LPDDR5X DRAM and modular chiplets. On the software side, the XRBench workloads run under a real-time OS (RTOS) or RT-patched Linux kernel, compiled through TVM or LLVM toolchains with specialized vector intrinsics to hit rigid 11\ ms frame deadlines at 90\ Hz [@HuzaifaEtAl2021ILLIXR].

Mobile XR is an ideal target because it forces us to juggle tight latency, thermal, and energy constraints alongside complex cross-layer behavior. We simply cannot optimize a single kernel or hardware block while turning a blind eye to the software pipeline, the memory system, or the rigid frame deadlines that users actually experience [@HuzaifaEtAl2021ILLIXR]. Early bringup of this software stack and ISA contract relies on tools like Spike, the canonical RISC-V ISA functional simulator, and Renode, an open-source multi-node system emulator, to verify compiler behavior before hardware implementation begins.

When we bring industrial integration into the picture, the stakes get even higher. We know that an accelerator in a modern system-on-chip (SoC) isn't a clean-sheet island; it has to plug into existing intellectual property using strict protocols like AMBA AXI.[^fn-axi-c01] If we design a candidate that boasts amazing power, performance, and area (PPA) metrics but botches a simple AXI handshake, we haven't built something we can actually integrate.

[^fn-axi-c01]: **AMBA AXI**: An Arm-defined on-chip interface protocol with separate channels and strict valid-ready handshake requirements [@Arm2020AXI]. A block that violates the protocol cannot be integrated into a system that depends on that interface, no matter how good its isolated power and performance numbers look.

We use the word *prompt* here for a reason, it's intentionally modest. A prompt expresses our high-level, compact intent. From there, we derive requirements that interpret the prompt's obligations and highlight the choices we still need to make. A true specification goes further, locking down enough behavior, interfaces, workloads, software semantics, constraints, and acceptance criteria to make our implementation testable. We then craft a study plan that pins down the reference design, alternative options, tools, budgets, and stopping conditions for a specific comparison. Right now, our Lighthouse request isn't a specification. Terms like "XRBench-class," "3\ W," "3\ nm-class," and the broad compute options we've allowed still demand concrete versioned workloads, software paths, reference designs, process assumptions, and verification checks. As architects, we have to pull those open choices out into the light before this request can drive real engineering, deciding exactly which interpretation makes it into the spec and what a successful result looks like.

Crucially, this prompt doesn't imply we'll just fire off a single model query and call it a day. Answering it requires a memory trace gathered from a fixed XRBench workload and configuration, a compiler built to target our proposed organization, an accurate simulator, a synthesis run mapped to a low-power library, and expert reviewers who can verify that the results actually back up our recommendation. Throughout this book, we are studying that entire human-plus-technical workflow, rather than just grading the fluency of a single generated response.

To properly study this workflow, we need to pin down exactly what we mean by *architecture* and *architect*. For us, architecture is far more than a clever microarchitecture, a high-level block diagram, or a physical chip artifact.

> **Architecture.** Architecture is the hardware and software contract and system organization turning workload intent and technology constraints into a defensible system design. It includes the instruction set architecture (ISA), microarchitecture, memory, interconnects, accelerators, chiplets, compiler and runtime interfaces, and deployment model.

> **Architect.** The architect is responsible for the architecture
> recommendation within the project's decision structure. The architect frames
> the problem, chooses abstractions, sets the evidence standard, integrates
> cross-layer results, and forms the supported technical recommendation.
> Specialists qualify measurements and checks and own technical signoffs in
> their domains. A separately named commitment authority decides whether the
> architecture advances to the next consequential transition. One person may
> hold more than one role, but the project must identify each responsibility
> and approval right.
> Methods can contribute candidates and analysis without assuming these
> responsibilities.

When we apply these definitions to the Lighthouse, we are committing to a comprehensive hardware-and-software result, not just a standalone chip. Any specific investigation we run still has to lock in the workload version, the hard deadlines, the architecture and software paths, our reference design, process libraries, operating assumptions, toolchains, budget, stopping conditions, implementation constraints, verification duties, and exact measurements. If we change a fixed condition, we completely alter the challenge; when we finally resolve an open choice, we make the project executable. While these choices make our design comparisons possible, they aren't the architecture itself. Ultimately, we must be ready to defend how those decisions support our comparison and our final technical recommendation.
### Decomposing Intent into Executable Specifications {#sec-intent-vs-spec}

When we look closely at the Lighthouse request, we see it spanning the entire stack because its compact wording conceals two distinct levels of work. We have to first translate its phrases into concrete architecture requirements, and then build a tool-connected comparison that supports our final technical recommendation (@fig-moonshot-prompt).

![**A compact prompt hides a full architecture study.** The prompt implies architecture requirements and engineering work that we must complete before we can form a supported result and technical recommendation.](images/F1-moonshot-stack){#fig-moonshot-prompt width="85%" fig-alt="Stacked diagram with the full Lighthouse prompt at the top, architecture requirements in the middle, and the execution and analysis requirements needed to support an answer at the bottom."}

Of course, architecture requirements cannot magically run a compiler or simulator on their own. We must connect our accepted workload, software, hardware, physical, reliability, and verification obligations to represented study state, tools, measurements, and checks (@fig-moonshot-prompt). As we run these tools, the results often force us to circle back and revise those very obligations. This hidden, tool-connected labor reminds us that we are not dealing with a simple prompt-to-chip automation pipeline.

[]{#sec-why-the-prompt-spans-the-stack}

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

Let us start with the prompt itself. We must translate high-level intent into guiding questions and coupled design choices long before we ever see a generated chip artifact. The prompt asks us to compare several compute organizations for a real-time mobile XR workload, ensuring we respect a 3\ W TDP[^fn-tdp-c01] budget and the realities of an LP process. As we break it down, individual phrases bound different parts of our study.

[^fn-tdp-c01]: **TDP (thermal design power)**: This book treats the Lighthouse target as a 3\ W sustained thermal envelope that the declared form factor and cooling assumptions must be able to remove, rather than as a peak instantaneous draw.

For instance, when we read "64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem," that fixes our word length and ISA family. Yet, in our study, we must still choose the exact ISA extensions (such as RVV 1.0 vector lengths or custom NPU matrix instructions), ABI[^fn-abi-c01], compiler, runtime, and software contract. Similarly, the phrase "XRBench-class real-time mobile XR workload" sets our target environment. We also notice the "accelerator block" provision, which intentionally leaves several compute organizations open for comparison – ranging from scalar RISC-V CPUs to decoupled vector pipelines and specialized systolic NPU engines. Meanwhile, the 3\ W target and 3\ nm-class LP process impose hard physical limits, helping us swiftly rule out any unfeasible proposals. To hit a 3\ W TDP in a mobile XR form factor, we have to explicitly state our cooling and skin-temperature assumptions, our packaging and signaling strategies, and exactly how much of that power budget we can allocate to the proposed compute subsystem versus off-chip LPDDR5X DRAM access energy (~100\ pJ per access vs ~0.1\ pJ per 32-bit ALU operation).

[^fn-abi-c01]: **ABI (application binary interface)**: The binary-level agreement on register usage, calling conventions, stack layout, and data alignment that lets separately compiled code interoperate. Adding a custom instruction changes the ISA, but shipping it means the compiler, libraries, and operating system have to agree on the ABI as well, which is why an ISA extension is a software project rather than a hardware edit.

Even though the prompt formally asks for a design-space report, our study might also produce software, models, RTL, layouts, prototypes, or even a physical chip, depending on how ambitious our claims are. Our final report weaves these artifacts and measurements into the proposed design, carefully explaining precisely why we rejected the alternatives. To really test our judgment, the prompt deliberately leaves the accelerator microarchitecture, memory system, software integration, and evaluation tools entirely open for us to define.

Turning these choices into a rigorous study requires us to formulate explicit constraints that our tools can actually ingest. We navigate requirement translation by combining profiling, analytical models, prior designs, design tools, and our own expert judgment. A simple product request like "we need a low-power AR headset" does not magically hand us a 3\ W TDP, point us to a particular RISC-V extension, or tell us the ideal L2 capacity. Instead, we must derive these study parameters ourselves, leaning heavily on workload and system evidence.

We can leverage learned methods to assist us here. They can extract candidate constraints from requirement documents, relate them to prior designs and public benchmarks, and flag ambiguities for us to resolve. For example, when a prompt vaguely asks for a "real-time" workload, a language model might push us to clarify whether we mean a strict 11 millisecond frame deadline at 90\ Hz, a 20 millisecond motion-to-photon bound, or a 99th-percentile tail-latency target.

However, this AI assistance does not eliminate our formulation work. While it can slash the time we spend assembling candidate specifications, we still make the final call on whether the proposed bounds are complete and supported. Before we can even begin our search, we must represent our accepted constraints in a format our tools can actually use, like a parameterized generator configuration or a sweep specification. We know all too well that prose alone cannot define a legal design space.

If we look at @tbl-moonshot-decomposition, we can see how each fragment of the Lighthouse prompt implies a cluster of architectural decisions and the checks that could ultimately disqualify an answer. Even if an automated method suggests a hardware and software decomposition, we remain the ones who must accept, revise, or outright reject that proposed scope and its coupled interfaces.

| **Prompt fragment** | **Architectural decisions** | **What must be checked** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **XRBench mobile XR** | Workload slice, input distribution, quality-of-service target, latency deadline, memory traffic, software pipeline, and drift assumptions. | Trace source, benchmark version, documented workload-phase selection, and rejection when results over-optimize a single hot loop or miss real-time behavior. |
| **64-bit RISC-V with vector or accelerator option** | ISA boundary, custom extension policy, programming model, compiler/runtime path, library support, and software compatibility. | Correctness, toolchain support, generated-code evidence, portability checks, and rejection of unsupported software semantics. |
| **Compute subsystem** | CPU, vector, or accelerator organization; memory hierarchy and interconnect; system integration; interface compatibility; and relevant reliability or isolation assumptions. | Design-space comparison and rejection of candidates that only win by moving cost, bandwidth, energy, complexity, or risk elsewhere. |
| **3\ W, 3\ nm-class low-power envelope** | Power, voltage and frequency, thermal and area limits, implementation constraints, and the hardware and software interfaces used for power management. | Source, version, and calibration of the power model; physical-design limits such as voltage drop, wire reliability, and timing closure; sensitivity analysis; and rejection criteria for throttling or reliability failures. |
| **Design-space report with evidence and rejected alternatives** | Alternatives, the Pareto frontier (the set of objective outcomes of feasible designs for which no alternative is at least as good on every objective and strictly better on at least one) [@Deb2001MultiObjective], assumptions, uncertainty, verification plan, rejected or failed candidates, and points at which the responsible architect decides whether to continue. | Measurements linked to assumptions and checks, rejected candidates, coverage, reproducible artifacts, and a named person responsible for the recommendation. |

: **A compact prompt hides multiple architecture decisions and independent checks.** The Lighthouse request expands into workload definition, software and ISA contracts, hardware organization, physical feasibility, and the checks that can reject an answer. {#tbl-moonshot-decomposition} tbl-colwidths="[18,34,35]"

We cannot settle the decisions in this table independently. A single shift in our workload, software, hardware, or physical choices can alter the validity of all the others, changing the very checks that might disqualify an answer. Consequently, the table acts to expand our requirements rather than cleanly completing a specification. We consider any answer incomplete if it fails to identify its workload slice, software contract, physical assumptions, supporting observations, and ultimately, the owner of the recommendation. Whenever we propose a commitment, we must explicitly identify the named authority standing behind it.

As we dive deeper, we find the workload and process phrases demand far more detail than the compact prompt initially provides. Fortunately, the XRBench suite gives us a concrete workload anchor to hold onto, rather than leaving us with a vague application label. End-to-end XR research reminds us just how tightly perception and display stages are coupled, turning mobile XR into a full system-level architecture target rather than just a single kernel for us to optimize [@HuzaifaEtAl2021ILLIXR]. Here again, we can use learned methods to analyze dataset distributions and uncover coverage gaps, beautifully complementing our traditional profiling, trace analysis, and expert workload judgment. For instance, an AI method could analyze a memory trace collected from a fixed XRBench workload and configuration, clustering access patterns to suggest specific cache hierarchies or local scratchpads for our simulations.

We must ensure our selected benchmark truly represents our broader system claim. Likewise, the prompt states the process node as a broad class rather than pointing us to a named foundry process design kit (PDK)[^fn-pdk-c01]. Even though we saw 2024 mobile SoCs publicly described in 3\ nm-class technology [@Apple2024A18Pro; @Apple2024M4], our study must explicitly name the specific process, libraries, voltage assumptions, and signoff path. We cannot support a true physical-feasibility claim until each surviving candidate successfully navigates the relevant physical-design flow.

[^fn-pdk-c01]: **PDK (process design kit)**: The package for one manufacturing process that supplies device models, design rules, and related data used by implementation tools. The open SKY130 PDK demonstrates that a PDK can be published [@SkyWater2020SKY130PDK], but it cannot supply the authorized project-specific information for a different process or commercial tool flow.

Ultimately, this short prompt hides a staggering amount of engineering depth. In our early studies, we might screen candidates against the "3\ W, 3\ nm-class" constraint using calibrated analytical models or partial implementations. However, any candidate we use to anchor a physical-feasibility claim must eventually run the gauntlet of relevant RTL, synthesis, floorplanning, timing, voltage-drop, leakage, thermal, and signoff checks. To evaluate these candidates with high fidelity, architects use gem5, a cycle-accurate architectural simulator, to analyze cache line contention, DRAMSim3, a cycle-accurate memory system simulator, to model LPDDR5X memory bus contention under XRBench frame traffic, and FireSim, an FPGA-accelerated cycle-exact hardware simulation platform based on Chipyard, to validate full-system real-time deadlines at hardware speed. Similarly, when we compare the RISC-V vector and accelerator alternatives, we must rigorously check the compiler, runtime, libraries, generated code, and overall software portability. Often, we find the software stack acts as our limiting dependency. A novel spatial accelerator is simply dead silicon if we cannot co-adapt the compiler to target it. To successfully meet these demanding workload and physical requirements, we must build a design system that keeps our knowledge, tools, and review loops tightly connected across the entire stack.
## System Architecture and Model Representations

### Architecture Foundation Models vs Project State

To carry our Lighthouse question across the stack, we need more than just reusable model knowledge. Our technical systems must actively maintain the current project state and weave together learned and conventional methods. We also have to connect these methods seamlessly to our compilers, simulators, implementation tools, and verification pipelines, ensuring we always return results that can be checked independently of whatever method produced the candidate.

We typically see the foundation-model pattern begin with broad training, followed by adaptation across various downstream tasks [@BommasaniEtAl2021FoundationModels]. Here, an *architecture foundation model* serves as a broadly pretrained learned component that we adapt across multiple architecture tasks. While it supplies valuable reusable prior knowledge, it does not hold the authoritative live project state, nor does it act as a complete design system on its own. Instead, we rely on an *AI-assisted design system*, a configured technical ensemble of learned and conventional components, tools, maintained state, feedback loops, and rigorous checks. Beyond this technical layer, our complete workflow encompasses human setup, intervention, review, repair, budget management, and the crucial decisions of when to stop. Once the technical system returns its checkable results, we, the architects, form a supported technical recommendation, leaving the separate commitment authority to decide whether the design advances to the next major milestone. Depending on the problem, we might use a single foundation model, several specialized models, or no learned models at all. Ultimately, our moonshot focuses on what this complete workflow can accomplish, rather than getting caught up in the name or scale of any individual model.

We can harness reusable learning to tackle several architecture tasks without replacing the rest of our trusted design system (@fig-foundation-system). We draw on our prior architecture artifacts and results, we can support a single learned component that adapts to numerous tasks. Meanwhile, we keep our current workload, constraints, candidate designs, tool versions, and measurements entirely separate within our version-controlled project record. This record maintains machine-readable specifications, SystemVerilog RTL descriptions, C++ behavioral models for Verilator, an open-source C++ HDL simulator, and physical design scripts for open-source flows like Yosys and OpenROAD alongside commercial synthesis and physical layout tools like Synopsys Design Compiler and Cadence Innovus. While that record serves as the authoritative source for what our study actually used, we still need to qualify its contents, keeping in mind that they can occasionally be wrong.

![**A foundation model is one optional component of the design system.** Reusable architecture knowledge can support a learned component adapted to workload analysis, prediction, generation, or diagnosis. The current project record, conventional methods, compilers, simulators, EDA and formal tools, and our independent checks remain part of the larger system. We supply our intent and constraints, review the supported result, and form a supported technical recommendation. A separate commitment authority decides whether our project advances, holds, or rejects that recommendation.](images/F1a-foundation-system){#fig-foundation-system width="100%" fig-alt="Reusable architecture knowledge feeds an optional architecture foundation model inside an AI-assisted design system. A separate version-controlled project record informs the active architecture tasks and conventional methods. Task outputs reach design tools and checks, which return evidence and update project state. A supported architecture result leaves the technical system for review by the architecture role, which forms a supported technical recommendation for a separate commitment authority."}

In the context of our Lighthouse challenge, this reusable component might help us analyze XR workloads, screen candidate organizations, draft software or RTL, or quickly diagnose a failed check. By contrast, our live study supplies the immediate context, including the current trace, our 3\ W envelope, the specific candidate identity, and the exact tool and library versions we are running. These current inputs fundamentally determine what our simulators, implementation tools, and verification flows actually evaluate; no amount of reusable prior knowledge can substitute for them.
## Evaluation Framework: Artifacts, Results, and Tradeoffs

### Qualifying Artifacts into Verifiable Results

A request doesn't become an architecture result in a single step. Instead, our work moves through a deliberate progression, starting from an initial request to requirements and specifications, into generating candidate artifacts, taking measurements, performing checks, and finally producing a comparative architecture result. From there, we build a technical recommendation that drives a commitment decision. These stages must remain distinct. We define an *artifact* as anything produced during the work (such as code, RTL, a model, a layout, a report, or a testbench). A *candidate* is a proposed design or configuration we want to compare. A *measurement* (or *observation*) gives us information about a candidate under stated conditions. Crucially, an *architecture result* is a supported comparison or finding where our assumptions, conditions, checks, alternatives, and limits are clear enough to inform our next action. We then integrate that result into a technical recommendation and choose the next steps for study. The named commitment authority ultimately decides whether the architecture advances to the next consequential transition. A valid architecture result doesn't always mean a breakthrough; it can reject every candidate, support retaining our current design, narrow the scope of the question, or simply conclude that our available measurements cannot decide the issue.

These distinctions help us determine how to allocate our scarce evaluation feedback. As architects, we might begin with a memory-trace slice collected from a fixed XRBench workload and configuration, alongside its software pipeline. We might propose alternatives, such as varying vector widths, swapping CPUs, or adding accelerators, and screen them with a cheap proxy. We reserve our expensive compiler, simulator, RTL, and physical-design effort, we ensure we only evaluate candidates whose results could actually alter our next action or technical recommendation. To do this rigorously, we must state our selection rules and the specific claim each check supports before we ever run the tools.

The distance between an artifact and a result is especially large in hardware. A generator might produce a mathematically elegant instruction extension that perfectly passes behavioral simulation, only to fail logic equivalence checking, design-rule checks, timing, power, or thermal limits during implementation. We can use a surrogate model[^fn-surrogate-model-c01] to cheaply screen candidates, but a design selected by the surrogate may still fail once a more faithful tool exposes properties the surrogate missed. This gap is our version of the simulation-to-real problem extensively studied in machine learning [@TobinEtAl2017DomainRandomization].

[^fn-surrogate-model-c01]: **Surrogate model**: A cheaper approximation of an expensive evaluation that lets a method screen many candidates quickly [@ForresterSobesterKeane2008Surrogate]. Its score is only a proxy, so a promising candidate still needs a higher-fidelity check before it can support a design decision.

Once we have measured the affected workload fraction and stated our mapping assumptions, Amdahl's law supplies an inexpensive rejection bound. For example, an accelerator that covers 60 percent of the XR pipeline's cycles inherently caps our whole-system speedup at 2.5 times, no matter how infinitely fast we make the block itself [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor]. When we profile memory traces and instruction counts on Spike, the canonical RISC-V ISA simulator, we can compute these bounds in seconds long before launching multi-hour microarchitectural simulations. Of course, this bound doesn't verify our profile, mapping, overlap, memory behavior, or implementation. We must also recompute the bound anytime a candidate changes the covered work or the underlying software path.

The roofline model supplies our second screening bound by relating operational intensity to peak compute and memory bandwidth [@Williams2009Roofline]. Much like the Amdahl calculation, this screen remains inexpensive only after we have measured or declared the specific inputs and assumptions that define the bound.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The roofline rejects a candidate before the simulator sees it"}
**Context.** The roofline bounds attainable performance once the study has a
candidate-specific operational intensity and the platform's peak compute and
memory bandwidth, which set its machine balance.

**How assistance uses the screen.** Generation can propose legal vector
configurations, prediction can estimate their data-movement risks, and
optimization can choose which configurations merit simulation. A candidate
whose bound is already inadequate need not enter the simulator queue.

**Required conditions and checks.** Operational intensity must reflect the
candidate's mapping, declared memory boundary, and cache or scratchpad
behavior. The study must recompute the bound when those properties change and
must still verify the mapping and resulting design for surviving candidates.

**Takeaway.** The roofline can reject an implausible candidate cheaply; it
cannot establish that the final design works.
:::

Analytical bounds, proxy scores, simulator results, and EDA reports provide very different kinds of evidence, at sharply different costs. We often see a proxy rank candidates one way, only for a simulator to completely overturn that ranking, while an EDA run might give us complex timing paths and congestion heatmaps rather than a convenient single score. For instance, BOOM-Explorer highlights that some implementation evaluations can take hours to run [@BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer]. In physical hardware, tools like Cadence Joules or Synopsys PrimePower, industry-standard gate-level power estimation engines, expose dynamic voltage drops and peak thermal hot spots that fast surrogate models completely miss. Iterative searches demand many trials before we can confidently distinguish the best actions. When our evaluation capacity cannot cover those trials, brute-force approaches simply blow past our budget. Statistical overfitting[^fn-overfitting-c01] provides a useful analogy here, though our specific failure mode is more acute. If we run a repeated search against a fast proxy, the search can exploit the proxy's omissions or errors. This produces apparent design gains that instantly evaporate when our surviving candidates finally hit a higher-fidelity tool.

[^fn-overfitting-c01]: **Overfitting**: The machine-learning failure of fitting the noise of a training sample so closely that performance does not generalize to new data [@HastieTibshiraniFriedman2009Elements]. Proxy exploitation is analogous but not identical; it can occur when search uses omissions or errors in an evaluator even without fitting a statistical model.

Crucially, our evaluation doesn't end just because a candidate clears its current checks. Hardware commitments freeze key choices on a timeline that stretches far beyond the rapid evolution of workloads, compilers, libraries, and learned models. As optimizers, we cannot safely specialize a 3\ nm-class accelerator to a single static trace without deeply considering how the workload and its software stack might shift before deployment. We must continually balance aggressive specialization with enough baseline programmability to ensure our designs actually survive that interval.

Even after bounds, proxies, and search tools narrow down our work, their output alone never proves whether a compiler assumption holds, whether the measured behavior truly stems from our proposed mechanism, or whether the remaining tradeoff supports the next consequential transition. Our studies should always record the candidates, assumptions, measurements, checks, and rejections that affect our core claims, without necessarily hoarding every internal model trace. We need to write a concise rationale that connects our proposals, tool results, rejected alternatives, and the final recommendation, keeping this rationale clearly distinct from the raw measurements. This practice helps reviewers spot missing assumptions, hidden contradictions, or conclusions that our checks simply don't support. We then rely on these recorded results and rationales to shape our technical recommendations or decide on the next phase of study.

Ultimately, a useful result must clear a much higher bar than a mere artifact. The measurements we take must support a fair comparison under explicitly stated conditions, and our checks must rigorously back up the final conclusion. We must record important alternatives and failures so that the result directly informs our next architecture action. Rejecting a candidate, choosing to retain our current architecture, or opting for a conventional method are all highly useful results in their own right.

These useful results don't need to conquer the entire Lighthouse challenge all at once. We can make real progress by closing out one clearly defined piece without claiming an end-to-end answer. A full-scope result addresses the complete challenge, yet it might still conclude that no candidate actually works. Even then, that outcome doesn't automatically establish the contribution of any named component or guarantee the broader success of the Architecture 2.0 program. Achieving full Lighthouse success demands a supported design that satisfies our fixed conditions alongside the complete design-space report promised by the prompt. This includes delivering the software path, meeting physical constraints, documenting rejected alternatives, proving applicable reliability and security properties under our declared fault and threat models, completing all checks, and providing a recommendation that an independent architect can critically examine.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Qualify artifacts before asserting results"}
A candidate, RTL block, report, or tool output is merely an unverified artifact
until qualified by measurements and checks under stated conditions. Never treat
a syntactically valid script or a successful local tool return as evidence that
an architecture should change. A valid architecture result must explicitly
identify the candidate, workload, measurement, check, and bounding conditions.
Only when this verified evidence can inform a specific architecture action does
an artifact become a result.
:::
### Multi-Metric Tradeoffs and Rejectable Evaluation Loops {#sec-efficiency-claims-need-rejectable-loops}

Even if our configured AI-assisted design system can produce a candidate and a polished report, we still need a scoped comparison to support a system claim. The difference between a plausible candidate and a defensible design becomes especially clear here, because we cannot judge the Lighthouse subsystem from a single score. Depending on workload behavior, software support, data movement, physical limits, verification effort, and deployment conditions, we might prefer completely different designs.

When we talk about efficiency, we are making a strict claim about how well a particular architecture performs useful work using limited resources. To make that claim, we must name the exact design, workload, and resource budget it covers. After all, a faster design fails to solve our problem if it blows past the power budget, defies verification, or relies on fragile software assumptions.

But a complete architecture result spans far more than efficiency alone. In quantitative computer architecture, we treat performance, cost, and power as first-class concerns [@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach]. As Dennard scaling weakened, dark silicon emerged, and multicore scaling hit its limits, we had to rely increasingly on specialization [@DennardEtAl1974Scaling; @BorkarChien2011FutureMicroprocessors; @EsmaeilzadehEtAl2011DarkSilicon; @JouppiEtAl2017TPU; @ChenEtAl2016Eyeriss; @HennessyPatterson2019GoldenAge]. That shift toward specialized hardware also meant we could no longer ignore broader system effects.

Data movement perfectly illustrates why we need this broader comparison. In the cited 45\ nm data, a 32-bit integer add costs about 0.1\ pJ, while SRAM and DRAM accesses cost orders of magnitude more [@Horowitz2014Energy]. In our 3\ nm-class Mobile XR SoC, where off-chip LPDDR5X DRAM accesses burn significant energy relative to on-chip NPU matrix multiplication, data movement across the AMBA AXI5 interconnect dominates the 3\ W TDP envelope. We must evaluate an accelerator that adds memory traffic with a system energy comparison rather than a compute-only claim, using tools like DRAMSim3, a cycle-accurate memory system simulator, coupled with gem5, a cycle-accurate architectural simulator, to capture true system-level energy. When we scale up to the warehouse level, our boundary expands to include utilization, networking, power delivery, operations, and total cost of ownership [@BarrosoHolzleRanganathan2019DatacenterAsComputer]. If we look at operational and embodied carbon, we have to add assumptions about manufacturing, energy mix, utilization, geography, and system lifetime [@GuptaEtAl2021ChasingCarbon]. We should include only the dimensions relevant to our specific claim, and we must explicitly name the violations, such as design-rule-check (DRC) failures or thermal limits, that completely rule out a candidate.

Furthermore, a valid comparison must account for our failed and rejected alternatives, not just our winning designs. We keep those negative results, we prevent future architects from wasting time reevaluating candidates that our earlier evidence already ruled out. Documenting our failures also clearly shows exactly which parts of the design space our claim actually covers.

Modern benchmark suites already report several of these dimensions at once. For example, MLPerf Inference, part of our community effort to make machine-learning performance claims reproducible across systems, includes deployment scenario, latency, throughput, and accuracy in its comparisons [@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf; @ReddiEtAl2020MLPerfInference]. We must always evaluate useful work against whatever resource is actually scarce in our stated setting, whether that happens to be latency, throughput, energy, power, area, cost, carbon, reliability, verification effort, engineering time, or project risk.

Ultimately, our design, workload, scenario, and scarce resource together define what "efficient" really means. For our Lighthouse system, a candidate that improves average throughput might still be a terrible choice if it misses an XR frame deadline, exceeds our 3\ W envelope under sustained load, or adds verification work that our project simply cannot absorb. If we change any of those conditions, we fundamentally change our claim and the evidence we need to support it.

To structure this comparison, we separate five dimensions of the architecture result from the cost of the study we used to reach it (@tbl-efficiency-dimensions). The first five rows judge our proposed system. The final row judges the evidence and engineering effort we required to establish that result. As architects, we should select the dimensions that define our claim and carefully check where a gain in one area might shift cost or risk somewhere else.

| **Dimension** | **Question** | **Why it complicates the comparison** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Performance** | How much useful work is delivered per unit time, latency budget, or service-level target? | The answer depends on workload selection, scenario, software stack, and whether the measured behavior matches the deployment claim. |
| **Power and energy** | How much useful work is delivered per watt, joule, thermal budget, or battery envelope? | A credible comparison must account for activity, data movement, voltage/frequency choices, thermal constraints, and fidelity gaps between estimates and signoff. |
| **Reliability and correctness** | Which required behaviors hold across faults, corner cases, nondeterminism, and the declared operating conditions? | A faster candidate is not acceptable if it spends its savings on fragility, security side-channels, debug burden, or invalid software and hardware assumptions. |
| **Scalability and cost** | How much useful work is delivered per dollar, rack, network hop, operator action, or unit of capacity? | Local wins can shift cost to memory, network, power delivery, utilization, operations, or total cost of ownership. |
| **Sustainability** | How much useful work is delivered per unit of operational and embodied environmental footprint? | Carbon depends on hardware lifetime, manufacturing, energy mix, utilization, and where and when computation runs. |
| **Study cost: evidence and engineering effort** | How much decision-relevant evidence is obtained per simulation, experiment, verification run, or engineer-hour? | Generating more candidates can still be inefficient if evaluation consumes scarce feedback, hides failures, or cannot reject weak outputs. |

: **A system result and the work needed to establish it require different measures.** Five dimensions describe the proposed system, while evidence and engineering effort describe the study. A valid comparison must show when an apparent improvement shifts cost or changes the scope. {#tbl-efficiency-dimensions} tbl-colwidths="[22,32,34]"

Reducing the cost of our study is valuable only if our remaining observations can still distinguish between alternatives and expose the failures that actually matter to our final decision.

Because these dimensions interact, we cannot tune them in isolation. In the mobile XR setting anchored by XRBench and ILLIXR, frame latency, energy, sustained power, and data movement are so tightly coupled that a gain in one area can easily violate a deadline or thermal limit in another. We might offset better simulated performance with crippling verification work, or we might achieve lower energy only by relying on fragile software assumptions. A candidate that looks like a winner under a proxy might completely fail when we test it on a more faithful workload. Therefore, we must explicitly explain which tradeoffs are acceptable for our stated constraints, defining the true scope of our system claim instead of hiding behind a single attractive artifact or score.

Even with these coupled requirements, we do not need AI for every architecture project. We often prefer conventional architecture methods when our design question and permitted changes are narrow enough to evaluate directly, and when our required feedback remains cheap and dependable. We should always start by identifying what our familiar models, scripts, simulators, and expert reviews already handle well, before we dictate exactly what we expect AI to improve. The real test is whether AI assistance leads us to a better system or a more reliable conclusion, rather than just helping us generate more artifacts.

When we look at measured RTL-generation benchmarks, we see substantial functional-test failures among generated candidates, making our independent checks absolutely essential [@VerilogEval; @PinckneyEtAl2024RevisitingVerilogEval]. The practical question is whether our complete approach, and all its required checks, actually improves the architecture result, lowers the total cost of reaching a result of comparable quality, or both, relative to competent conventional work. If every bad proposal forces us into a multi-hour synthesis run, our evaluation pipeline can easily consume more engineering time and computation than the AI method ever saved us.

Our Lighthouse prompt makes this friction concrete. The requested subsystem must support a specific workload class, meet a strict power envelope, fit our technology assumptions, interact correctly with our software stack, and produce reviewable evidence. When we make our final comparison, we must carefully weigh energy, latency, memory traffic, programmability, verification, and deployment risk. While a single scalar objective might help an automated search navigate this complex space, it can never substitute for our architectural judgment.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{11\baselineskip}
```
## State of the Art and Benchmark Assessment

### Survey of AI-Assisted Design Systems

When we survey the public examples available through July 2026, we see impressive individual capabilities rather than a complete end-to-end answer. We can better understand their strongest claims by making the checks behind each result explicit. For each system, we must ask what artifact it produced, what test could reject it, how much of the broader architecture problem that test actually observes, and what we can inspect from the outside. We follow those checks, we reveal both our progress and the remaining gaps, without mistakenly treating fundamentally different systems as steps in a single ranking.

Exact or inexpensive checks let us support strong claims over a narrow task. For example, AlphaTensor found a 4 by 4 matrix-multiplication algorithm for a two-element domain that uses 47 scalar multiplications rather than Strassen's 49 [@FawziEtAl2022AlphaTensor]. Because every candidate admitted an exact algebraic check, the system could confidently accept or reject solutions. Similarly, AutoTVM evaluates many tensor-program schedules on real hardware; we can measure the result directly, and most failures stay safely contained inside the tuning run [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. While these reliable checks make search highly practical, neither result gives us a complete system architecture.

When we rely on proxy and simulator feedback, we can support broader exploration, though we inherently adopt the limits of our checking models. We see AlphaChip use wirelength and congestion proxies to guide macro placement [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. Meanwhile, ArchGym demonstrated that no single search algorithm dominates across our design spaces when we hold simulators and sample budgets fixed [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym]. To reduce costly target evaluations, Apollo transfers knowledge across related accelerator design spaces, whereas BOOM-Explorer pays hours per sample to execute a documented 7\ nm flow [@yazdanbakhsh2021apollo; @BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer]. We find each result meaningful within its chosen feedback source, yet we require stronger evidence before any of them can support a wider physical or system claim.

Functional tests, post-synthesis metrics, and fabricated silicon establish vastly different levels of hardware progress. Since functional success alone cannot guarantee hardware design quality, we look to systems like VerilogEval to check functional behavior [@VerilogEval; @PinckneyEtAl2024RevisitingVerilogEval], while RTLLM layers on post-synthesis design-quality measures, though still stopping short of physical signoff [@RTLLM].
Pushing further, Chip-Chat reached tapeout for a small processor through extensive human-guided revision, and Enlightenment-1 produced a fabricated RISC-V core by automating an iterative verification-and-revision loop [@BlockloveEtAl2023ChipChat; @ChengEtAl2024AutomatedCPU]. We view these as substantial implementation achievements, yet neither system manages to deliver the full multi-tool system-architecture capability our moonshot demands.

We find human ratings and proprietary deployment reports much harder to evaluate from the outside. For instance, ChipNeMo reports task-specific internal gains, ChatEDA checks tool execution alongside human-rated request fulfillment on 50 ChatEDA-Bench tasks via a simplified OpenROAD wrapper, and DSO.ai announces 100 commercial tapeouts without publishing a matched methodology [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo; @HeEtAl2024ChatEDA; @Synopsys2023DSOai]. While these reports clearly show our community moving learned methods into real workflows, they cannot single-handedly establish independent functional correctness, guarantee complete physical signoff, or prove a net benefit over a strong alternative.

Together, these examples demonstrate remarkably useful pieces of a broader design capability. We can use learned search and measured autotuning to explore our choices; we can leverage placement and RTL generation to produce physical artifacts; we can build tool-using systems to invoke real flows; we can rely on domain adaptation to support selected engineering tasks; and we can push generated designs all the way to silicon under tightly bounded conditions. Our moonshot aims to connect these demonstrated capabilities through current project states and appropriate design tools, all while retaining independent checks robust enough to reject an unsound result. We recognize that no single example has established that complete system yet.

Across these systems, we see that any given result only truly supports the specific claim its check can inspect. When we step back, we realize that check cost and fidelity, task scope, baseline quality, workflow coverage, and access to supporting material all fundamentally limit what we as architects can conclude (@tbl-existing-systems).

| **System** | **What it establishes** | **The telltale limit** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AlphaTensor [@FawziEtAl2022AlphaTensor] | Learned search improved a fifty-year-old matrix-multiplication count for 4 by 4 matrices modulo two | The algebraic construction admits an exact mathematical check, and a single scalar scores it |
| AutoTVM [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM] | Measured search can improve schedules when many candidates run quickly on real hardware | The result covers tensor-program schedules, where failures usually remain safely contained within the tuning run |
| AlphaChip [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment] | A learned policy produces macro placements a production flow accepts | The reward relies on proxy wirelength and congestion, and the matched baseline remains disputed |
| ArchGym [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym] | At equal sample budgets no search algorithm dominates, so our chosen harness and budget ultimately shape the result | Because every candidate is graded by a simulator, the result inherently adopts its fidelity limits |
| Apollo and BOOM-Explorer [@yazdanbakhsh2021apollo; @BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer] | Learned design-space exploration can successfully exploit domain-specific evidence | Apollo transfers knowledge across related accelerator spaces to reduce costly target evaluations; BOOM-Explorer uses an open-source core but depends on commercial tools and pays hours per sample |
| VerilogEval and RTLLM [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM] | We can measure RTL generation on shared tasks | VerilogEval emphasizes functional simulation; RTLLM adds post-synthesis quality metrics; neither actually reaches physical signoff |
| Chip-Chat and Enlightenment-1 [@BlockloveEtAl2023ChipChat; @ChengEtAl2024AutomatedCPU] | Generated logic has reached silicon, including a core that successfully boots Linux | One relies on extensive human-guided revision; the other demonstrates an automated processor implementation and verification loop, rather than the full multi-tool system-architecture capability our moonshot poses |
| ChatEDA [@HeEtAl2024ChatEDA] | An agent can plan and invoke a real tool flow directly from stated intent | The benchmark checks tool execution and human-rated request fulfillment on 50 ChatEDA-Bench tasks using a simplified OpenROAD wrapper, lacking independent functional correctness or complete signoff |
| ChipNeMo [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo] | Domain adaptation can improve selected internal engineering tasks | The gains remain task-specific, general models stay stronger on certain subtasks, and outsiders cannot reproduce the proprietary evaluation |
| DSO.ai [@Synopsys2023DSOai] | Learned flow-parameter search has reached 100 vendor-reported commercial tapeouts | The evidence standard remains a press release, lacking any public methodology or matched baseline |

: **The strength of each result depends on its scope and how we evaluate it:** Exact, inexpensive checks support strong scoped claims, whereas narrow measurements, proxies, weak baselines, and hidden supporting data, methods, or artifacts all limit what we can ultimately conclude. {#tbl-existing-systems} tbl-colwidths="[20,37,43]"

We present this table as a set of scoped claims, not as a definitive ranking of systems. We embrace shared tasks, we make it vastly easier to inspect exactly where each claim stops. For example, ImageNet [@RussakovskyEtAl2015ImageNet] armed computer vision with a transformative common benchmark, while CASP (Critical Assessment of Structure Prediction) [@MoultEtAl1995CASP] forced AlphaFold's [@JumperEtAl2021AlphaFold] structure predictions to face a rigorous community-held assessment. These powerful precedents prove the immense value of common tasks and checks, yet they never absolve us from the need to carefully qualify what our domain-specific checks actually establish.

We can draw a useful contrast with software engineering, where a public test harness can return a task-level result much faster than our hardware designs can ever obtain physical evidence. We turn real GitHub-issue fixes into a shared task graded by automated repository tests, SWE-bench gives our coding systems a relatively quick and repeatable signal (@fig-swebench-progress) [@JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench]. When a system passes those tests, it supports a claim about resolving the specific issue under benchmark conditions, rather than guaranteeing complete software correctness. While our hardware processes also enjoy fast checks for specific properties, our complete system-and-chip claims must painstakingly connect functional verification with synthesis, timing, power, physical-design, and thermal evidence, each varying wildly in cost and fidelity.

```{python}
#| label: fig-swebench-progress
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Standardized task-level checks support rapid iteration on SWE-bench Verified.** Best reported SWE-bench Verified score [@JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench] for each model name in a dated snapshot of Epoch AI's benchmarking hub [@EpochAI2025AIModels]; the line traces the best result to date. Reported configurations and test harnesses can differ, so the plot shows the pace of benchmark progress rather than a controlled comparison among models. Scores climbed from roughly a third of this human-filtered 500-task subset to over four-fifths in about seventeen months. Repository tests provide a quick, repeatable signal for the defined task, while a complete architecture claim must combine functional and physical evidence from several tools.
#| out-width: "88%"
#| fig-alt: "Scatter of the best reported SWE-bench Verified resolved percentage for each model name versus model release date from late 2024 to 2026. Points climb from about 31 percent to about 84 percent, with a solid line tracing the best-to-date frontier."

import csv
import datetime
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Data: SWE-bench Verified results [@JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench] tracked in Epoch
# AI's benchmarking hub [@EpochAI2025AIModels]; best score per model name in
# the dated snapshot. Values dataset-transcribed. Accessed 2026-07-19.
# Receipt: data/source-receipts/chapter1-swebench-verified.csv
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]

def _yfrac(text):
    for fmt in ("%Y-%m-%d", "%Y-%m", "%Y"):
        try:
            d = datetime.datetime.strptime(text.strip(), fmt)
            return d.year + (d.timetuple().tm_yday - 1) / 365.25
        except ValueError:
            continue
    return None

pts = []
with open(_root / "data" / "source-receipts" / "chapter1-swebench-verified.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    for row in csv.DictReader(fh):
        x = _yfrac(row["release_date"])
        try:
            score = float(row["resolved_fraction"])
        except ValueError:
            continue
        if x is None:
            continue
        pts.append({"model": row["model"], "score": score * 100 if score <= 1 else score, "x": x})

# The snapshot can contain several configurations under the same model name.
# Retain only the best reported score for each name rather than presenting
# those configurations as distinct model releases.
best_by_name = {}
for p in pts:
    name = (p["model"] or "").strip()
    if name not in best_by_name or p["score"] > best_by_name[name]["score"]:
        best_by_name[name] = p
pts = list(best_by_name.values())
pts.sort(key=lambda p: p["x"])
best = -1.0
frontier = []
for p in pts:
    if p["score"] > best:
        best = p["score"]
        frontier.append(p)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 3.2))
ax.scatter([p["x"] for p in pts], [p["score"] for p in pts], s=16, marker="o",
           facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.7, zorder=2, label="Named models")
ax.plot([p["x"] for p in frontier], [p["score"] for p in frontier], color=COLORS["evidence"], lw=1.6, zorder=3)
ax.scatter([p["x"] for p in frontier], [p["score"] for p in frontier], s=22, marker="o",
           facecolor=COLORS["evidence"], edgecolor=COLORS["evidence_ink"], linewidth=0.5, zorder=4, label="Best to date")
ax.set_xlim(2024.8, 2026.55)
ax.set_ylim(20, 92)
ax.set_xlabel("Model release date", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_ylabel("SWE-bench Verified resolved (%)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_xticks([2025.0, 2025.5, 2026.0, 2026.5])
ax.set_xticklabels(["2025", "mid-25", "2026", "mid-26"], fontsize=6.4)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.4, length=2.5, width=0.6)
for _sp in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[_sp].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(True, which="major", axis="y", color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=0)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", frameon=False, fontsize=6.0, handletextpad=0.3, labelspacing=0.3)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.10, right=0.97, top=0.98, bottom=0.12)
```

We cannot isolate model, harness, or system effects from this trend (@fig-swebench-progress), because our retained receipt only records reported values rather than a controlled evaluation protocol, and a later OpenAI audit ultimately withdrew SWE-bench Verified from frontier capability measurement [@OpenAI2026SWEBenchLimits]. Nevertheless, it brilliantly demonstrates how a standardized, automated task-level check can support rapid iteration across our models and engineering systems. In our architectural work, we also use fast analytical, structural, and functional checks, but no single check ever closes a complete system-and-chip claim. Our early screens routinely leave timing, design-rule, power, and thermal feasibility roughly estimated or entirely untested. To confidently assert physical feasibility, we must eventually run the relevant implementation-facing checks. While our static analysis and calibrated proxies can reduce these costs by actively screening candidates, they can never fully replace them.

Fortunately, our discipline already has shared checks at individual layers. We have seen SPEC-style benchmarks make performance claims far more comparable through common workloads, strict run rules, and precise reporting standards, effectively steering which improvements we choose to pursue as a community [@Patterson2012Benchmarks; @SPEC2017CPU]. We rely on gem5, a cycle-accurate microarchitectural simulator, and FireSim, an FPGA-accelerated cycle-exact hardware simulation platform, to provide shared simulation platforms at different costs and fidelities [@BinkertEtAl2011Gem5; @KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. We also rely on Verilator, an open-source high-performance C++ HDL simulator, for fast functional verification of custom RISC-V vector extensions. Similarly, MLPerf defines rigorous benchmark suites and submission rules for our machine-learning systems [@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf]. These vital resources ensure that we as outside researchers can rerun, compare, and challenge any scoped result. However, they do not render our results automatically correct, nor do they connect all the diverse evidence we require for the Lighthouse. We must therefore view our current systems as establishing bounded progress toward our moonshot, rather than delivering a definitive, end-to-end verdict.
### Data Scarcity, Verification Load, and Generators vs. Verifiers {#sec-data-scarcity-verification-load}

Our moonshot vision hinges on highly specific, often scarce project data, the very details that connect our high-level architecture choices to tangible physical results. Just as importantly, it relies on having enough verification muscle to rigorously test these hardware candidates once we produce them.

While public software repositories easily expose source changes, technical discussions, and testing frameworks, hardware is far more guarded. ChipNeMo, for instance, relies on proprietary software, RTL, verification testbenches, specifications, and internal documentation [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo]. If we lean solely on models trained on public text for our architecture studies, we might generate plausible-looking RTL that completely misses our specific interfaces, PDKs, memory subsystems, or signoff constraints. Open designs and open PDKs certainly help, but they cannot replace the authorized PDK, IP blocks, and precise tool configurations required to actually evaluate our project's physical claims.

Moreover, technical fit isn't our only hurdle when using project data, our candidates must also survive intense legal and compliance scrutiny. If our model generates RTL by blindly regurgitating code from its training set without strict provenance tracking, we expose our designs to inbound IP contamination. Conversely, if we send proprietary specifications, constraints, or EDA tool reports out to an unauthorized model endpoint, we risk catastrophic outbound disclosure. Without strict data isolation and clear provenance, our AI-generated architectures will never clear legal signoff, instantly wiping out any speedups we gained during candidate production. We must constantly manage source permissions, output provenance, project confidentiality, and outside-review access as distinct, non-negotiable requirements for how we handle data.

Fortunately, we do not have to rely on training data alone to fill these information gaps. As architects, we can actively supply specifications and analytical models, encode our own machine-checkable constraints, pull in live documentation, and use tool feedback to refine our candidates iteratively. For example, RTLFixer showcases how we can use tool-guided repair following syntax and compiler feedback [@TsaiEtAl2024RTLFixer]. Similarly, Chipyard bridges shareable RISC-V designs to simulation and implementation paths [@chipyard], and OpenROAD offers us an open digital physical-design flow [@AjayiEtAl2019OpenROAD]. In large-scale verification, we combine Verilator for rapid C++ co-simulation with FireSim for FPGA-accelerated cycle-exact verification of full 64-bit RISC-V SoC cores and NPU matrix engines under realistic XRBench trace inputs, alongside formal tools like Synopsys Formality for equivalence checking. While these platforms brilliantly illustrate how we can expose constraints and harness feedback, they cannot magically recover the proprietary information that lies beyond their reach.
