We dive deeper into the mechanisms for building and representing this critical project knowledge in @sec-data-representations-world-models.

Even if we perfect candidate generation, we still face the massive hurdle of verification. A first-pass RTL candidate might look completely plausible while hiding subtle, fatal errors. In fact, industry surveys show that verification eats up roughly half of our total engineering effort, with our design engineers dedicating nearly half of their own time just to verification tasks [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. We can certainly leverage reusable UVM[^fn-uvm-c01] environments across multiple related candidates, but our stimulus, checkers, assertions, coverage models, and debug capacity must constantly evolve to match the new behaviors our generated candidates introduce. If our candidate production speeds past our ability to test, our primary bottleneck simply shifts directly to verification. Ultimately, generating hardware faster only matters if we retain the ability to rigorously identify and reject bad candidates at that same accelerated pace.

[^fn-uvm-c01]: **UVM (Universal Verification Methodology)**: A standardized methodology and class library for building reusable SystemVerilog verification environments, including stimulus, monitors, scoreboards, and coverage components [@IEEE2020UVM].

Furthermore, our verification efforts must push well beyond basic functional correctness, especially when our design's threat model involves hardware security. As Spectre infamously demonstrated, processors that are functionally flawless can still bleed data through microarchitectural side channels [@KocherEtAl2019Spectre]. If we use AI to generate security-relevant hardware, we are obligated to apply independent checks tailored to our specific design and threat models. This means we must proactively verify isolation properties, run side-channel analyses, and hunt for malicious modifications. While our generation models can certainly help us draft SystemVerilog assertions, outline security properties, and build testbenches, they absolutely cannot prove their own correctness.

Because we constantly battle scarce project information and exorbitant verification costs, maintaining explicit state becomes an absolute requirement for AI-assisted architecture. Our automated components demand that we provide the current candidate, constraints, permitted actions, and tool outputs in a strictly machine-usable format. Likewise, our human reviewers need clear access to measurements, failed checks, and underlying assumptions so we can properly judge the AI's recommendations. None of this replaces our established architectural practices. Rather, it dramatically changes exactly what our practices must expose and track when we invite learned methods into our design loops.
### Architecture 1.0 to Architecture 2.0 {#sec-from-architecture-10-to-architecture-20}

We use Architecture 1.0 as shorthand for our established, human-directed practice. We already rely on analytical models, scripted flows, automated search, parameterized generators, simulators, synthesis, optimization, and verification. Architecture 2.0 retains this foundation while allowing learned methods to take on selected roles across more of our work [@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20]. This distinction focuses on the breadth and role of AI participation, rather than just swapping manual effort for automation (@tbl-arch1-vs-arch2).

| **Feature** | **Established architecture practice (Architecture 1.0)** | **AI-assisted architecture practice (Architecture 2.0)** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Problem framing | Architects define the question, abstractions, constraints, and tool tasks | Learned methods may help interpret broader intent or incomplete information and propose choices for architect review |
| Exploration | Architects use analytical models, scripts, parameterized generators, sweeps, and conventional optimization | Prediction, generation, and learned optimization may propose, screen, or select alternatives alongside established methods |
| Tool use | Architects and scripts invoke simulators and design tools, preserve results, and decide what to run next | Automated components may select later actions from tool returns, so state, cost, failures, and permitted actions must be usable by the component and inspectable by the reviewer |
| Result standard | Measurements and checks turn candidate artifacts into comparisons that can support the next architecture action | The same standard applies; broader automated participation does not make an unchecked artifact an architecture result |
| Recommendation and commitment | Architects integrate results and form the technical recommendation; a named commitment authority decides whether the architecture advances to the next consequential transition | Methods may organize analysis or prepare a draft recommendation, while the architect and commitment authority retain their respective responsibilities |

: **AI participation broadens what may be delegated without changing the authority structure.** Architecture 2.0 adds learned prediction, generation, optimization, retrieval, or tool coordination to established analytical and automated practice while the architect retains the technical recommendation and a named commitment authority decides whether the architecture advances to the next consequential transition. {#tbl-arch1-vs-arch2}

Inviting AI into our process does not automatically generate explicit evidence or sound record-keeping. In our conventional projects, we already preserve requirements, artifact versions, tool databases, verification results, rejected candidates, and architectural decisions. We typically distribute this project knowledge and state across engineering artifacts and our own expert practice. When we introduce automated components, we must explicitly represent the selected state and permitted actions for machine use while ensuring our reviewers can still inspect them (@fig-design-loop-breaks).

![**Automated participation adds a machine-use requirement.** Our established architecture work can retain explicit evidence while our project knowledge remains distributed across specifications, source code, tool databases, verification artifacts, and expert practice. When we add automated components, we must also represent selected state and permitted actions for machine use while keeping them inspectable by our reviewers. Both panels retain a review point and a feedback path; neither assigns organizational commitment to that review step.](images/F2a-design-loop-breaks){#fig-design-loop-breaks width="85%" fig-alt="Two side-by-side diagrams compare established human-orchestrated and AI-assisted architecture studies. The left distributes project knowledge across engineering artifacts, records, and expert practice. The right also represents selected state and permitted actions for automated methods. Both panels retain explicit evidence, expert or architect review, and a feedback path without assigning organizational commitment to the review step."}

We must keep this machine-usable state strictly aligned with the artifacts and records our reviewers inspect. Meeting this requirement does not automatically validate the outputs, nor does it transfer our responsibility for the technical recommendation or our commitment authority.
<!-- Generators and Verifiers integrated into Evaluation Framework -->

We must deliberately coordinate our methods to keep every local action tied to our original design question. If we don't, a generator, surrogate, simulator, or implementation tool might succeed locally but end up advancing the wrong candidate, or missing a crucial system obligation entirely.

To manage this, our design system keeps the architecture question and its obligations current alongside candidate, tool, and version state. From there, we assign prediction, generation, optimization, or conventional methods based on whatever work is currently limiting our progress. We use tool feedback and independent checks to constrain their outputs, while leaning on cost and clear stopping conditions to bound the overall effort.

Critically, we must keep candidate production separate enough from checking to actually expose failures. Even nominally independent implementations often fail on the exact same hard inputs [@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion], and multiple components can easily repeat the same flawed assumption if they share training data, a proxy, or an underlying model. In this book, we treat an *independent check* as a strict operational threshold. Under this threshold, the method that produces a candidate neither controls its check nor acts as the sole pass/fail authority. Likewise, the check cannot simply inherit its decisive assumptions and implementation straight from the generator. While achieving complete independence is rare, we know that a check only repeating its producer's assumptions can never truly qualify our results.

Ultimately, even when we coordinate a study perfectly, it cannot definitively establish whether our proposed architecture succeeds or if our complete approach actually improves the work. To make those final judgments, we need entirely separate tests.
## Operationalizing the Moonshot: Evaluation, Pitfalls, and Research Frontiers

### The Two Moonshot Evaluation Tests

We evaluate our moonshot against two distinct tests. The first isolates the architecture itself, while the second assesses the impact of our complete human-plus-technical workflow.

**Architecture result.** We first ask whether a study proves that a proposed design satisfies the fixed Lighthouse conditions. Does this design justify itself against the architecture reference when subjected to our required workload, software, implementation, physical, and verification checks? We might conclude that a new design is objectively better. We might recommend keeping the original reference. Alternatively, we might find that none of our available options actually meet the necessary conditions.

**Complete AI-assisted approach.** Next, we evaluate the entire process. We compare our AI-assisted approach against the strongest practical conventional or human-directed workflow. We must rigorously match the starting information, tool access, total budget, human work accounting, and stopping conditions. Under those constraints, we ask a simple question. Did our complete approach improve the final architecture result, reduce the total cost of achieving a comparable result, or both?

Separating these two tests drives several critical consequences for how we measure success. A brilliant design does not automatically prove that our AI-assisted workflow improved the engineering process. Conversely, an inexpensive process never justifies an inferior architecture. If a conventional workflow produces a sound result, we still count that as a success for the architecture question even if our complete approach failed to beat it. Furthermore, while a random search gives us a useful performance floor, we cannot assume it represents the strongest practical conventional baseline.

Notice that neither of these comparisons isolates the contribution of a specific foundation model, generator, surrogate, or individual software component. If we want to make that narrower claim, we must perform a controlled replacement or ablation study within an otherwise identical system. When we call these tests "independent," we simply mean they answer fundamentally different questions. We do not imply that their measurements are statistically independent.

When we zoom out to assess the broader program, we do not invent a third test. Instead, we aggregate repeated comparisons of our complete approach across various tasks, design stages, and conditions. To claim program-level success, our complete approach must consistently improve architecture results, reduce the cost of achieving comparable quality, or both across our entire declared scope. Based on the public evidence we reviewed for this edition, we cannot yet settle that final verdict.

A single successful Lighthouse study gives us an existence proof. It does not provide broad validation for a completely new design method. To achieve that, our same two tests must hold up across all our declared tasks and conditions. Independent teams must be able to reproduce our relevant measurements and supported results using our preserved inputs, tools, and checks. Finally, those outside teams must have the ability to deeply inspect the engineering basis behind any technical recommendation we make.
### Common Architectural Pitfalls

When adopting AI-assisted methods or evaluating moonshot proposals, it is easy to conflate a local win with a system victory. The following pitfalls highlight where unverified assumptions, misapplied metrics, or incomplete boundaries lead to flawed architectural conclusions:

**Confusing Artifacts with Results.** Mistaking a generated block of RTL or a syntactically correct script for an architecture decision. A valid result must be checked against workload, software, and physical constraints before it can support a commitment.

**Ignoring the System Boundary.** Optimizing an isolated component, such as an accelerator, without accounting for data movement, memory bandwidth limits, or strict interface constraints (like AXI handshakes). A faster block that violates system integration is not a solution.

**Overfitting to Proxies.** Using surrogate models or fast proxy metrics to repeatedly optimize a design, only to find the "gains" disappear when subjected to higher-fidelity verification tools. Proxy exploitation creates apparent progress that physical tools later reject.

**Conflating Method Success with Architecture Success.** Celebrating a fast AI-assisted generation step even if the total end-to-end cost (including verification and human review) is higher, or the final architecture is inferior. The method's speed does not automatically justify the resulting architecture.

### Open Research Questions

The transition from generating isolated artifacts to establishing a verifiable, AI-assisted design capability marks a fundamental expansion in what our discipline can reliably build. The frontier of this chapter lies precisely at the gap between compact system intent and rigorous cross-stack validation, a space where current design automation breaks down. Resolving how we capture unstructured requirements, enforce physical constraints, and prevent proxy exploitation across the full hardware-software contract requires more than incremental tool updates. These are foundational challenges worthy of a PhD thesis or dedicated research paper. Because this moonshot opens questions that no single design study can settle, this first set asks what the larger Architecture 2.0 effort must make possible to advance our discipline, setting the stage for the specific open questions that conclude every subsequent chapter.

**Building a usable design capability.** The moonshot requires both an
executable description of the current architecture problem and reusable
knowledge that can help without displacing authoritative project state.

- **How can compact system intent become an executable architecture
  specification without losing system obligations?** The specification must
  carry workload behavior, software semantics, interfaces, physical limits,
  and acceptance conditions into tools even when the original request leaves
  some of them implicit. We must discover how to expose those missing
  obligations without replacing the architect's intent with assumptions made
  by the system.

- **What architecture knowledge can transfer across projects, and how can a
  design system detect when it no longer applies?** Prior designs can save
  repeated work, yet their assumptions may fail silently after workloads,
  software, tools, or implementation conditions change. The discipline's
  challenge is to make that loss of applicability visible before reused
  knowledge produces an unsupported architecture result.

**Establishing progress toward the moonshot.** Architecture 2.0 must improve
the resulting architecture, reduce the total cost of reaching a comparable
result, or do both.

- **Where does AI assistance create net value after its complete cost is
  counted?** A faster local step may not reduce the complete effort once data
  preparation, simulation, verification, failed work, and human review are
  included. The unresolved question for practitioners and researchers alike
  is whether assistance improves the final architecture result, lowers the
  total cost of reaching it, or merely moves work elsewhere.

- **What minimum evidence should accompany a claimed Architecture 2.0
  advance?** Architecture results often depend on proprietary designs, tools,
  and physical data that cannot be disclosed, yet outside reviewers, and
  students learning the practice, still need enough information to challenge
  the claim. A useful disclosure boundary must protect restricted material
  without making the claimed advance impossible to assess.

### Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Mandate explicit specifications before commitment"}
A compact request is never a specification. Before treating any request as an
executable target, explicitly define the workload, software contract, system
boundary, legal alternatives, physical limits, acceptance checks, and intended
decision. While provisional assumptions allow early exploration, they strictly
cannot support architectural commitment. An isolated candidate may falsely
appear superior if the comparison omits a critical dependency or constraint.
Ensure every reported measurement traces to a verified evidence path before
committing to a design.
:::

The Lighthouse request gives the moonshot a fixed system-and-chip target
across workload, software, hardware, implementation, physical constraints,
verification, and the final recommendation. A coordinated design system may
use foundation or specialized models, prediction, generation, optimization,
retrieval, conventional algorithms, and tool-connected environments. None of
those components is the moonshot by itself. The capability lies in carrying
the architecture question through the complete work to a checked result,
technical recommendation, and separately owned commitment decision. It would
qualify as a useful new design method only if it makes that larger design object
expressible, executable, and checkable by people other than its creator.

The two tests keep the claims separate. The architecture comparison asks
whether a supported design meets the Lighthouse conditions. The comparison of
the complete approach asks whether assistance improves the result, lowers the
total cost of reaching a comparable result, or both. Current systems show
meaningful progress on individual tasks, but their evaluation cost, fidelity,
scope, and access to supporting material limit what they establish about the
complete challenge.

The moonshot matters only if present-day architecture work has become difficult
enough that additional assistance is worth investigating. The next chapter
examines the compounding sources of that difficulty
(@sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales).
